extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and scholars of political philosophy, history, and literature (readers of the Encyclopédie)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the merit, method, style, and historical reasoning of major political-philosophical works (exemplified by Montesquieu's writings). Useful for literary criticism, historiography, and philosophy-of-law appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of a vast and obscure subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should render an immense, confused subject (laws, customs, institutions of nations) intelligible and ordered; demonstrate success in tackling a subject of great difficulty and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eulogy praises Montesquieu for bringing 'belle lumière' to an enormous, confused field and for daring to 'débrouiller' and bring to principles a subject previously seen as chaos. Merit is measured by the capacity to reduce complexity into intelligible principles despite the subject's vastness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a scientific/modern spirit to political and social facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat political and social phenomena with a modern, scientific approach rather than as purely moralizing or juridical commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu is credited as the first to apply the modern/scientific spirit to political facts (likened to Descartes or Newton in method). The work should analyze causes, relations, and regularities among institutions rather than only comment on laws as texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain laws by underlying causes/principles (not merely comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper study of laws seeks the reasons for laws in principles external to the law itself (government principles, character of people, religion, customs, population, luxury, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses that 'commenter une loi, ce n'est point en donner la raison' and that the critic must discover causes among many possible influences and reduce them to a small number. Evaluation should check whether the author uncovers and connects these causal factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to interrelations among principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that principles may be causes or consequences of one another and that they modify each other (e.g., religion and government, luxury and population).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should assess whether an author examines principles both in isolation and together, accounting for reciprocal influence and chains of causation rather than treating principles as independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful division and classification of subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should exhibit an order in its large parts and in details: each object assigned to the division it exclusively belongs to, and overlapping topics placed where they properly belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eulogy defends Montesquieu's apparent lack of method by showing there is an internal order: the author should follow a consistent system and not scatter topics arbitrarily. Good division makes visible influences among parts like branches of a well-understood tree of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real disorder from apparent disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Real disorder exists when analogy and sequence of ideas are not observed or when conclusions are erected as principles; apparent disorder is acceptable when intermediate ideas are intentionally omitted for readers who can supply them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring should check whether perceived disorganization is substantive (breaks logical sequence or circularity) or deliberate concision aimed at thoughtful readers. The evaluator should identify misplaced conclusions or genuine structural faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate clarity/obscurity for intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity is permissible when the book targets thinking readers who are expected to supply omitted links; obscurity that hides confusion for ordinary readers is a defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eulogy argues that what is obscure for vulgar readers may not be so for the intended intelligent audience; thus assessors must consider the intended readership when judging clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness combined with intellectual depth
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should be able to treat many subjects briefly yet profoundly, selecting the fruitful branches and leaving much to stimulate the reader's thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu is praised for saying a great deal in small space and for exposing 'branches fécondes' without tediously detailing everything. Evaluation should reward productive brevity that provokes reflection rather than mere compression that omits essentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of authorities and factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid citing doubtful authorities or advancing controversial or false facts; rely on sound sources and careful factual foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eulogy notes Montesquieu 'a cité des autorités douteuses, avancé des faits controversés ou même faux' as a defect. Reviews should flag questionable citations and factual errors and weigh their impact on conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and appropriate scope of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles advanced must have appropriate generality and not be either too narrow in scope or overstretched beyond what they justify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu is criticized for sometimes giving his principles more reach than they merit and forgetting them; evaluation should examine whether principles are well-founded and consistently applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firmness in criticizing abuses when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong critical work should not be excessively timid in denouncing abuses and should exercise sufficiently firm critique where warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eulogy remarks Montesquieu's 'critique n'est point assez ferme contre quelques abus.' Assessors should note whether the author adequately confronts social/political abuses or soft-pedals important criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical method: combine imperfect materials with sound conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with ancient or fragmentary sources, the author should combine defective materials thoughtfully and use reasoned conjecture to reconstruct plausible accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text compares the historian to an architect tracing an ancient building from ruins: merit lies in combining imperfect data 'de la manière la plus vraisemblable' and supplementing with genius and happy conjecture, not in inventing unsupported facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on laws as they operate on real human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Place primary emphasis on how laws function in relation to the actual capacities, motivations, and social arrangements of people rather than on metaphysical ideals of perfect laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu's approach praises examination of what the law can practically oblige people to do and the human susceptibilities laws must address; reviewers should value pragmatic, human-centered analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounding by comparative observation and travel
rubrics_metrics.description: Good political-philosophical work is grounded in broad empirical observation: study of constitutions, laws, customs across nations, and conversations with notable contemporaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eulogy highlights Montesquieu's travels (Vienna, Italy, England, Holland) and conversations with major figures as preparation for his work. Evaluation should reward empirically grounded comparative insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhetorical devices (persona, satire) to reveal society
rubrics_metrics.description: Using fictional or foreign personae (e.g., Usbek in Lettres persanes) and satire can serve as an effective pretext to critique manners and institutions, provided attribution and intent are responsibly handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given to the technique of using an outsider's voice to expose domestic follies; critics should also caution against condemning authors without verifying authorship or context (the text warns against hasty denunciation based on misattribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity: emphasize fruitful lines rather than exhaustive detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer concentrating on the most fecund aspects of a subject instead of burdening the reader with all details; present branches that yield insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eulogy commends limiting detail to what is productive and leaving much to the reader's reflection. Assessment should value the discernment in choosing which facts and themes to develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible public critique (verify claims before condemning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public criticism should distinguish what the author truly wrote from interpolations or misattributed passages before condemning the work or the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recounts how denunciation of Montesquieu's Lettres persanes relied on 'un extrait infidèle' and stresses the importance of judging by reading rather than rumor or delation; reviewers should verify assertions and authorship.
